extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato's Republic; philosophy/classics students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting the evaluative standards and character/educational criteria Plato gives for philosophers, guardians, and states (from the ship-pilot parable through selection and education of rulers). Useful for literary or philosophical analysis of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: True philosopher: led by truth and love of being
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lover of knowledge is always striving after being — he will not rest in the multiplicity of individuals but will pursue the knowledge of the true nature of every essence; truth is his leader and failing in this he is an impostor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosopher's nature is defined by an unceasing desire for knowledge and 'becoming incorporated with very being.' He is not satisfied with opinions or appearances; he seeks the Form/absolute. Anti-pattern: one who studies only appearances or aims at opinion and praise rather than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher's virtues (justice, temperance, courage, magnificence, apprehension, memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: When properly formed, the philosopher's company will include justice and health of mind, temperance, courage, magnificence, apprehension, and memory; these are natural gifts of the true philosopher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues accompany the philosophic nature when it is genuine. The text repeatedly lists and appeals to these qualities as markers of authentic philosophers. Note: possession of these virtues can still be corrupted by environment or miseducation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher utterly hates a lie
rubrics_metrics.description: If truth is the captain, the philosopher will utterly hate a lie and cannot be suspected of evil when led by truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty and aversion to falsehood are intrinsic marks of the true philosopher. Anti-pattern: sophists who manipulate appearances and praise for gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler must combine authority with technical knowledge (pilot analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true pilot (ruler) must pay attention to seasons, sky, stars, winds and all that belongs to his art; the union of authority with the steerer’s art is required — he must be the steerer whether other people like or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority without technical/artistic knowledge is dangerous; likewise technical knowledge without rightful authority will be ignored. Example/anti-pattern: sailors who claim a right to steer without learning navigation and who denounce the true pilot as a 'star-gazer' or 'good-for-nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers are treated as useless because society refuses to use them
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who call philosophers useless are right insofar as philosophers are of no use to the world, but the fault lies with those who will not use them, not with the philosophers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social order and the unwillingness of the many to accept expert rulership produce the appearance of uselessness. Use the ship parable to explain this relational cause rather than blame philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: High virtues and goods can distract or corrupt philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: The very virtues (courage, temperance, etc.) and ordinary goods (beauty, wealth, strength, rank, connections) that are prized can, under improper conditions, destroy or distract the philosophic soul and lead it away from philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine natures are more sensitive to bad environments; great gifts can be misapplied into pride and politics. Anti-pattern: assuming external goods guarantee philosophic fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion/Sophists corrupt by teaching to please the many
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Sophists and the public teach nothing but the opinion of the many — they study the tempers and desires of the multitude and teach what pleases them, calling that wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast sophistry (catering to tastes of the mob) with genuine wisdom (apprehension of being). Example: a teacher who only learns how to soothe or inflame the great beast (the populace) and labels this as wisdom is a corrupter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry of unworthy persons into philosophy produces sophisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When those unworthy of education (imperfect natures or mere craftsmen) rush into philosophy attracted by its dignity, they produce sophisms captivating to the ear but with nothing genuine in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against superficial converts who adopt philosophical language as attire (like the tinker who bathes and puts on fine clothes) — their 'marriage' with philosophy yields bastard, worthless doctrines. Criterion for evaluating philosophers: provenance and seriousness of vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of philosophy requires a favorable State or compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy will not be esteemed nor flourish unless the State is suitable to it, or unless philosophers are providentially compelled to take care of the State, or princes/kings are divinely inspired with true philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either institutional receptivity or extraordinary compulsion/inspiration is required for philosophers to function as rulers and for the ideal constitution to emerge. The text calls the realization difficult but not impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of philosophers: life-stage structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical study should be lifelong and properly ordered: in childhood and youth study suited to tender years with bodily care; as intellect matures increase 'gymnastics of the soul'; when civic/military duties cease, permit unrestricted philosophic pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposes the common practice of treating philosophy as an occasional pastime. Emphasizes bodily training early, intellectual discipline later, and final leisure for free philosophical activity (mirrors the guardians' curriculum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection/tests for guardians/rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be lovers of their country tested by pleasures and pains — they must retain patriotism in hardships and dangers, be purified like gold tried in the refiner’s fire, and be examined by labours, dangers, pleasures, and multiple kinds of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection involves moral trials under pressure as well as intellectual examinations across diverse disciplines to ascertain endurance for the highest knowledge. Anti-pattern: appointing rulers based solely on birth or popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite character required: quickness and steadfastness together
rubrics_metrics.description: Those fit for higher education and office must combine quick intelligence, memory, sagacity, cleverness with steadfast, dependable natures (courage and immovability); both sorts of qualities are necessary but rarely found united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing must identify souls that can bear both intellectual toil and steadfastness in action; many have either quick intellect and restlessness or steadiness but intellectual torpor. This informs selection and training requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator/painter of constitutions must begin from a 'clean tablet' and imitate the divine pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Before inscribing laws the legislator must 'rub out the picture' (erase existing manners) and trace the constitution's outline by looking to absolute justice, beauty, and temperance and tempering human elements into the image of the divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law- and constitution-making should model human institutions on higher, immutable forms. Practical guidance: reform requires removing ingrained corrupt practices before building anew; this is difficult but defines the legislator's method.
